Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
note.paragraph: Meet BETSY, the Bovine Expert Tracking and Surveillance system developed by OneCup AI. BETSY helps ranchers keep a virtual eye on their cattle at all times.

Geoffrey Shmigelsky, an Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning specialist, sparked a transformative idea while sitting around a campfire at a family reunion. He asked Mokah Shmigelsky’s rancher cousins what they wanted AI to do for them, and the response was simple—identify each of our cows. This initial idea blossomed into BETSY, a sophisticated system that now monitors the health and wellness of cattle across the prairies of Canada and beyond.

BETSY’s monitoring process is thorough and detailed, providing ranchers with a sense of reassurance. Her “brain” is divided into levels. Ranchers install cameras to record digital videos of their herds, which are sent in real-time to BETSY’s computer system. In Level 1, BETSY draws a bounding box around each animal. Moving into Level 2, she identifies key points such as the animal's eyes, nose, hips, knees, hooves, and tail. By Level 3, she can identify which animal from the herd is in each specific box. She then monitors the animal’s behavior in Level 4. The first clue that something is amiss with an animal is a change in behavior. Level 5 involves analyzing the animal’s behavior over time and alerting the rancher to any significant differences that appear. By tracking the animal’s behavior, BETSY can detect changes in feeding, movement, or body stance, which may indicate that an animal is sick and needs care. BETSY sends an alert to the rancher’s cell phone if an animal shows signs of illness, shows up lame, or if a cow is going into labor and may need assistance as she delivers her calf.

image.alt: A diagram of BETSY’s monitoring process is shown.

note.paragraph: OneCup AI, responding to client requests and drawing from its own expertise, continues to enhance BETSY by teaching her new skills. But how does BETSY learn? She learns by watching training videos. During this supervised learning process, BETSY builds a model that is consistent with the information in the videos she has been given. For instance, BETSY watched videos to distinguish between cows in labor and those not in labor. This continuous learning process, which ensures that BETSY constantly improves and adapts to new challenges, instills confidence in her capabilities.

BETSY’s success is only as good as the data she is trained on. One of the more challenging programs inside BETSY involves deciding whether the animal in a photo or video is a cow, horse, sheep, or goat. When an Alberta Clipper blanketed the prairies (and animals) with white snow, BETSY suddenly identified a lot more “sheep” than she had the day before! Once BETSY had her training videos updated to include correctly identified animals covered in snow, she was no longer fooled by a few flakes.

Why stop at cattle on the prairies of Canada? One of the most useful features of mathematical techniques is that, once they have been developed, they are independent of their motivational source. The methods developed by OneCup AI to monitor cattle can be adapted to monitor other animals. For example, BETSY now has programs for monitoring the health and well-being of horses, sheep, pigs, cats, and dogs. Geoffrey and Mokah Shmigelsky are even talking to wildlife specialists in the Amazon, discussing the potential for BETSY to help monitor the health and wellness of wildlife living in the rainforest.

note.paragraph: According to Geoffrey, “At OneCup AI, we love linear algebra!” Like is done at OneCup AI, machine learning and AI comprise developing systems that interpret external data correctly, learn from such data, and use that learning to achieve specific goals and tasks through flexibility and adaptation. The foundational ideas for everything from digital video feeds to Deep Learning depend on linear algebra. In Section 6.2, we see a simple way to design a matrix so that matrix multiplication can identify a specified pattern of blue and white squares. In Sections 6.5, 6.6, and 6.8, we explore techniques used in machine learning.

intro.paragraph: Solving systems of equations has been a common theme throughout this text, but what happens when there are no solutions? A good approximation to a solution may still be enough to make sound decisions. A well-defined notion of nearness is needed to find an approximate solution to an inconsistent system of equations. Although the measure of “nearness” may change depending on the application, one notion of distance is introduced in Section 6.1, along with the notion of orthogonality. As illustrated in Sections 6.2 and 6.3, orthogonality can be used to simplify calculations and to identify the nearest point in a subspace $W$ to a specified point outside of $W$. By taking $W$ to be the column space of a matrix, in Section 6.5, a method for producing approximate (least-squares) solutions for inconsistent linear systems is developed, providing an essential technique in Machine Learning, which is discussed in Sections 6.6 and 6.8. Section 6.4 provides another opportunity to see orthogonal projections at work, presenting a matrix factorization widely used in numerical linear algebra. A more abstract view of orthogonality is given in Section 6.7, providing the flexibility needed to tailor the measure of “nearness” to the application.

content.heading: 6.1 Inner Product, Length, and Orthogonality
content.paragraph: Geometric concepts of length, distance, and perpendicularity, which are well known for $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ and $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, are defined here for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. These concepts provide powerful geometric tools for solving many applied problems, including the least-squares problems mentioned above. All three notions are defined in terms of the inner product of two vectors.
content.heading: The Inner Product
content.paragraph: If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then we regard $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ as $n \times 1$ matrices. The transpose $\mathbf{u}^{T}$ is a $1 \times n$ matrix, and the matrix product $\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$ is a $1 \times 1$ matrix, which we write as a single real number (a scalar) without brackets. The number $\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}$ is called the inner product of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, and often it is written as $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$. content.paragraph: The rest of this chapter depends on the fact that the concept of perpendicular lines in ordinary Euclidean geometry has an analogue in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.

Consider $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ or $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ and two lines through the origin determined by vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$. The two lines shown in Figure 5 are geometrically perpendicular if and only if the distance from $\mathbf{u}$ to $\mathbf{v}$ is the same as the distance from $\mathbf{u}$ to $- \mathbf{v}$. The two squared distances are equal if and only if $2\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = - 2\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$, which happens if and only if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$.

This calculation shows that when vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are identified with geometric points, the corresponding lines through the points and the origin are perpendicular if and only if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$. The following definition generalizes to $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ this notion of perpendicularity (or orthogonality, as it is commonly called in linear algebra).

note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Two vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ are orthogonal (to each other) if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0$.

content.heading: Orthogonal Complements
content.paragraph: To provide practice using inner products, we introduce a concept here that will be of use in Section 6.3 and elsewhere in the chapter. If a vector $\textbf{z}$ is orthogonal to every vector in a subspace $W$ of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then $\textbf{z}$ is said to be orthogonal to$W$. The set of all vectors $\textbf{z}$ that are orthogonal to $W$ is called the orthogonal complement of $W$ and is denoted by $W^{\bot}$ (and read as “$W$ perpendicular” or simply “$W$ perp”).

content.paragraph: Remark: A common way to prove that two sets, say $S$ and $T$, are equal is to show that $S$ is a subset of $T$ and $T$ is a subset of $S$. The proof of the next theorem that $\text{Nul~}A = \left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ is established by showing that $\text{Nul~}A$ is a subset of $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ and $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ is a subset of $\text{Nul~}A$. That is, an arbitrary element $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{Nul~}A$ is shown to be in $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$, and then an arbitrary element $\textbf{x}$ in $\left( \text{Row~}A \right)^{\bot}$ is shown to be in $\text{Nul~}A$.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. The orthogonal complement of the row space of $A$ is the null space of $A$, and the orthogonal complement of the column space of $A$ is the null space of $A^{T}$:

content.heading: Proof﻿
content.paragraph: The row–column rule for computing $A\textbf{x}$ shows that if $\textbf{x}$ is in $\text{Nul~}A$, then $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to each row of $A$ (with the rows treated as vectors in $\left. \text{ℝ}^{n} \right)$. Since the rows of $A$ span the row space, $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to $\text{Row~}A$. Conversely, if $\textbf{x}$ is orthogonal to $\text{Row~}A$, then $\textbf{x}$ is certainly orthogonal to each row of $A$, and hence $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$. This proves the first statement of the theorem. Since this statement is true for any matrix, it is true for $A^{T}$. That is, the orthogonal complement of the row space of $A^{T}$ is the null space of $A^{T}$. This proves the second statement, because $\text{Row~}A^{T} = \text{Col~}A$.

content.heading: Orthonormal Sets
content.paragraph: A set $\left\{ \mathbf{u}_{1}\text{,~}\ldots\text{,~}\mathbf{u}_{p} \right\}$ is an orthonormal set if it is an orthogonal set of unit vectors. By the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, $\mathbf{v}_{k + 1}$ is orthogonal to $W_{k}$. Note that $\text{proj}_{W_{k}}\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$ is in $W_{k}$ and hence also in $W_{k + 1}$. Since $\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$ is in $W_{k + 1}$, so is $\mathbf{v}_{k + 1}$ (because $W_{k + 1}$ is a subspace and is closed under subtraction). Furthermore, $\mathbf{v}_{k + 1} \neq \textbf{0}$ because $\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$ is not in $W_{k} = \text{Span}\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,}\textbf{x}_{k} \right\}$. Hence $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,}\mathbf{v}_{k + 1} \right\}$ is an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors in the $(k + 1)$-dimensional space $W_{k + 1}$. When $k + 1 = p$, the process stops.

Theorem 11 shows that any nonzero subspace $W$ of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ has an orthogonal basis, because an ordinary basis $\left\{ \textbf{x}_{1}\text{,}\ldots\text{,}\textbf{x}_{p} \right\}$ is always available (by Theorem 12 in Section 4.5), and the Gram–Schmidt process depends only on the existence of orthogonal projections onto subspaces of $W$ that already have orthogonal bases.

content.heading: 6.5 Least-Squares Problems
content.paragraph: Inconsistent systems arise often in applications. When a solution is demanded and none exists, the best one can do is to find an $\textbf{x}$ that makes $A\textbf{x}$ as close as possible to $\textbf{b}$.

Think of $A\textbf{x}$ as an approximation to $\textbf{b}$. The smaller the distance between $\textbf{b}$ and $A\textbf{x}$, given by $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$, the better the approximation. The general least-squares problem is to find an $\textbf{x}$ that makes $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$ as small as possible. The adjective “least-squares” arises from the fact that $\parallel \textbf{b} - A\textbf{x} \parallel$ is the square root of a sum of squares.

content.heading: 6.6 Machine Learning and Linear Models
Machine Learning
content.paragraph: Machine learning uses linear models in situations where the machine is being trained to predict the outcome (dependent variables) based on the values of the inputs (independent variables). The machine is given a set of training data where the values of the independent and dependent variables are known. The machine then learns the relationship between the independent variables and the dependent variables. One type of learning is to fit a curve, such as a least-squares line or parabola, to the data. Once the machine has learned the pattern from the training data, it can then estimate the value of the output based on a given value for the input.
content.heading: Least-Squares Lines
content.paragraph: A common task in science and engineering is to analyze and understand relationships among several quantities that vary. This section describes a variety of situations in which data are used to build or verify a formula that predicts the value of one variable as a function of other variables. In each case, the problem will amount to solving a least-squares problem.

For easy application of the discussion to real problems that you may encounter later in your career, we choose notation that is commonly used in the statistical analysis of scientific and engineering data. Instead of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$, we write $X\textit{\textbf{β}} = \mathbf{y}$ and refer to $X$ as the design matrix, $\textit{\textbf{β}}$ as the parameter vector, and $\textbf{y}$ as the observation vector.

The simplest relation between two variables $x$ and $y$ is the linear equation $y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$.1 Experimental data often produce points $\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$, $\ldots$, $\left( x_{n},y_{n} \right)$ that, when graphed, seem to lie close to a line. We want to determine the parameters $\beta_{0}$ and $\beta_{1}$ that make the line as “close” to the points as possible.

Suppose $\beta_{0}$ and $\beta_{1}$ are fixed, and consider the line $y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$ in Figure 1. Corresponding to each data point $\left( x_{j}\text{,~}y_{j} \right)$ there is a point $\left( x_{j}\text{,~}\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{j} \right)$ on the line with the same $x\text{-coordinate}$. We call $y_{j}$ the observed value of $y$ and $\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x_{j}$ the predicted $y\text{-value}$ (determined by the line). The difference between an observed $y\text{-value}$ and a predicted $y\text{-value}$ is called a residual.

content.paragraph: There are several ways to measure how “close” the line is to the data. The usual choice (primarily because the mathematical calculations are simple) is to add the squares of the residuals. The least-squares line is the line $y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}x$ that minimizes the sum of the squares of the residuals. This line is also called a line of regression of y on x, because any errors in the data are assumed to be only in the $y\text{-coordinates}$. The coefficients $\beta_{0}$, $\beta_{1}$ of the line are called (linear) regression coefficients.2

content.heading: 6.7 Inner Product Spaces
content.paragraph: Notions of length, distance, and orthogonality are often important in applications involving a vector space. For $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, these concepts were based on the properties of the inner product listed in Theorem 1 of Section 6.1. For other spaces, we need analogues of the inner product with the same properties. The conclusions of Theorem 1 now become axioms in the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: An inner product on a vector space $V$ is a function that, to each pair of vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $V$, associates a real number $\left\langle \mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$ and satisfies the following axioms, for all $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $\textbf{w}$ in $V$ and all scalars $c$:

list.item: ⟨cu, v⟩=c ⟨u, v⟩
⟨u, u⟩≥0 and ⟨u, u⟩=0 if and only if u=0

note.paragraph: A vector space with an inner product is called an inner product space .

content.paragraph: The vector space $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ with the standard inner product is an inner product space, and nearly everything discussed in this chapter for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ carries over to inner product spaces. The examples in this section and the next lay the foundation for a variety of applications treated in courses in engineering, physics, mathematics, and statistics.

Nevertheless, it is important to remember that each function is a vector when it is treated as an element of a vector space.

content.heading: The Gram–Schmidt Process
content.paragraph: The existence of orthogonal bases for finite-dimensional subspaces of an inner product space can be established by the Gram–Schmidt process, just as in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Certain orthogonal bases that arise frequently in applications can be constructed by this process.

The orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace $W$ with an orthogonal basis can be constructed as usual. The projection does not depend on the choice of orthogonal basis, and it has the properties described in the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem and the Best Approximation Theorem.

content.heading: Best Approximation in Inner Product Spaces
content.paragraph: A common problem in applied mathematics involves a vector space $V$ whose elements are functions. The problem is to approximate a function $f$ in $V$ by a function $g$ from a specified subspace $W$ of $V$. content.heading: An Inner Product for C[a, b] (Calculus required)
content.paragraph: Probably the most widely used inner product space for applications is the vector space $C\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$ of all continuous functions on an interval $a \leq t \leq b$, with an inner product that we will describe.

We begin by considering a polynomial $p$ and any integer $n$ larger than or equal to the degree of $p$. Then $p$ is in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$, and we may compute a “length” for $p$ using the inner product of Example 2 involving evaluation at $n + 1$ points in $\lbrack a\text{,~}b\rbrack$. However, this length of $p$ captures the behavior at only those $n + 1$ points. Since $p$ is in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ for all large $n$, we could use a much larger $n$, with many more points for the “evaluation” inner product. See Figure 4.

content.heading: Trend Analysis of Data
content.paragraph: Let $f$ represent an unknown function whose values are known (perhaps only approximately) at $t_{0}$, $\ldots$, $t_{n}$. If there is a “linear trend” in the data $f\left( t_{0} \right)$, $\ldots$, $f\left( t_{n} \right)$, then we might expect to approximate the values of $f$ by a function of the form $\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}t$. If there is a “quadratic trend” to the data, then we would try a function of the form $\beta_{0} + \beta_{1}t + \beta_{2}t^{2}$. This was discussed in Section 6.6, from a different point of view.

In some statistical problems, it is important to be able to separate the linear trend from the quadratic trend (and possibly cubic or higher-order trends). For instance, suppose engineers are analyzing the performance of a new car, and $f(t)$ represents the distance between the car at time $t$ and some reference point. If the car is traveling at constant velocity, then the graph of $f(t)$ should be a straight line whose slope is the car’s velocity. If the gas pedal is suddenly pressed to the floor, the graph of $f(t)$ will change to include a quadratic term and possibly a cubic term (due to the acceleration). To analyze the ability of the car to pass another car, for example, engineers may want to separate the quadratic and cubic components from the linear term.

If the function is approximated by a curve of the form $y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}t + \beta_{2}t^{2}$, the coefficient $\beta_{2}$ may not give the desired information about the quadratic trend in the data, because it may not be “independent” in a statistical sense from the other $\beta_{i}$. To make what is known as a trend analysis of the data, we introduce an inner product on the space $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ analogous to that given in Example 2 in Section 6.7. For $p$, $q$ in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$, define

paragraph.math: $$\left\langle p\text{,~}q \right\rangle = p\left( t_{0} \right)q\left( t_{0} \right) + \cdots + p\left( t_{n} \right)q\left( t_{n} \right)$$

content.paragraph: In practice, statisticians seldom need to consider trends in data of degree higher than cubic or quartic. So let $p_{0}$, $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$, $p_{3}$ denote an orthogonal basis of the subspace $\text{ℙ}_{3}$ of $\text{ℙ}_{n}$, obtained by applying the Gram–Schmidt process to the polynomials $1$, $t$, $t^{2}$, and $t^{3}$. There is a polynomial $g$ in $\text{ℙ}_{n}$ whose values at $t_{0}$, $\ldots$, $t_{n}$ coincide with those of the unknown function $f$. Let $\widehat{g}$ be the orthogonal projection (with respect to the given inner product) of $g$ onto $\text{ℙ}_{3}$, say,

Then $\widehat{g}$ is called a cubic trend function, and $c_{0}$, $\ldots$, $c_{3}$ are the trend coefficients of the data. The coefficient $c_{1}$ measures the linear trend, $c_{2}$ the quadratic trend, and $c_{3}$ the cubic trend. It turns out that if the data have certain properties, these coefficients are statistically independent.

Since $p_{0}$, $\ldots$, $p_{3}$ are orthogonal, the trend coefficients may be computed one at a time, independently of one another. (Recall that $c_{i} = \left\langle g\text{,~}p_{i} \right\rangle/\left\langle p_{i}\text{,~}p_{i} \right\rangle$.) We can ignore $p_{3}$ and $c_{3}$ if we want only the quadratic trend. And if, for example, we needed to determine the quartic trend, we would have to find (via Gram–Schmidt) only a polynomial $p_{4}$ in $\text{ℙ}_{4}$ that is orthogonal to $\text{ℙ}_{3}$ and compute $\left\langle g\text{,~}p_{4} \right\rangle/\left\langle p_{4}\text{,~}p_{4} \right\rangle$.
